concept.name: Vector Databases, HNSW Indexing & RAG Pipelines
concept.tagline: Perform high-dimensional approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) similarity search for AI LLM context retrieval.

spark.summary: Vector databases index high-dimensional vector embeddings (e.g. 1536-dim vectors) produced by AI models, enabling sub-millisecond semantic search via Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph indexing.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use HNSW graph indexing with Cosine Similarity or Dot Product metrics for fast RAG knowledge retrieval.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional B-Trees and relational indexes cannot search unstructured high-dimensional embeddings. Vector databases bridge LLM context windows with enterprise data.
whenNotToUse: Exact string lookups or traditional SQL primary key relational queries.
keyPoints: Embeddings map text or media into dense numerical vectors in high-dimensional vector space.
HNSW constructs multi-layer navigable small world graphs to achieve logarithmic O(log N) search latency.
RAG combines vector similarity retrieval with generative LLM prompt context.

examples.outcome: Pinecone/Qdrant retrieves top-5 vector chunks in 12ms.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 HNSW Graph Indexing & Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Relational B-Trees cannot efficiently query high-dimensional embeddings (e.g. 1536-dimensional vectors from OpenAI or Cohere) because the **Curse of Dimensionality** forces table scans. Vector databases (Pinecone, Milvus, Qdrant, pgvector) rely on **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)** indexing—most prominently **Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)** graphs.

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "HNSW Multi-Layer Search & RAG Context Pipeline",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "user", "label": "User Query", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "embed", "label": "Embedding Model", "type": "processor" },
    { "id": "hnsw", "label": "HNSW Top Layer (Sparse Skip-List)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "base", "label": "HNSW Base Layer (Dense Vectors)", "type": "database" },
    { "id": "llm", "label": "LLM Context Generator", "type": "processor" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "user", "to": "embed", "label": "1. Convert to Vector" },
    { "from": "embed", "to": "hnsw", "label": "2. Fast Entry Point Hop" },
    { "from": "hnsw", "to": "base", "label": "3. Greedy Local Search" },
    { "from": "base", "to": "llm", "label": "4. Inject Top-K Chunks into Prompt" }
  ]
}
```

### 🕸️ How HNSW Multilayer Graphs Work

HNSW extends probabilistic skip-lists into multidimensional graph spaces:

1. **Top Layers (Sparse Highway)**:
   - Only a fraction of vectors are promoted to upper layers ($l > 0$).
   - Traversal begins at the top entry point, executing rapid, long-distance hops across clusters to quickly home in on the query region.
2. **Bottom Layer (Layer 0 - Dense Network)**:
   - Contains 100% of the vector population connected by local Delaunay-approximated edges.
   - Executes greedy beam search to return the true Top-$K$ nearest neighbors based on Cosine Similarity or Dot Product.

### ⚖️ Vector Indexing Strategies: HNSW vs IVF-PQ

| Index Type | Search Latency | RAM Consumption | Recall Accuracy | Best Workload |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HNSW** | Ultra-fast (< 5ms) | High (must hold vectors + graph pointers in RAM) | > 98% recall | Real-time chat assistants, latency-critical RAG |
| **IVF-PQ** | Medium (10–25ms) | Low (compresses vectors into 8-bit quantization codes) | ~85–92% recall | Billions of embeddings, cost-constrained search |

### 🔍 Single-Stage Hybrid Search & Pre-Filtering

In enterprise RAG, vector distance alone is insufficient—queries must be constrained by metadata (e.g. `tenant_id = 'acme'` and `created_at >= 2024-01-01`).
- **Anti-pattern (Post-filtering)**: Finding Top-100 nearest vectors and then filtering by tenant often yields 0 valid results.
- **Production Pattern (Filtered HNSW)**: Graph traversal evaluates metadata constraints at each node evaluation hop, guaranteeing valid Top-$K$ retrieval.

questions.title: HNSW Vector Indexing Mechanics
questions.prompt: Why is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) preferred over brute-force k-NN (k-Nearest Neighbors) in production RAG systems?

options.text: HNSW converts numerical vectors into plaintext strings.
options.explanation: HNSW builds graph structures over vector embeddings, not plaintext conversion.

options.text: Brute-force k-NN scales linearly O(N), whereas HNSW builds a multi-layer graph that navigates to nearest neighbors in logarithmic O(log N) time.
options.explanation: Correct! HNSW transforms expensive linear scans into sub-millisecond graph traversals.
